title: Strong national well-being can coexist with an intergenerational gradient in work, mental health, and social connection
source_unit: OECD, Well-being along the life course in Finland: Implications for forward-looking policy design
geography: Finland, benchmarked against OECD countries and examined across young, middle-aged, and older life stages

aggregate_pattern.value: Finland performs strongly on many well-being dimensions, but aggregate strength masks an intergenerational gradient

younger_adults.value: younger people face rising unemployment, declining PISA performance, and deteriorating subjective well-being after the pandemic

policy_logic.value: forward-looking policy should target life-stage-specific risks instead of relying on national averages

observations.method: OECD multidimensional well-being assessment combining aggregate indicators, peer benchmarking, life-course breakdowns, and forward-looking policy analysis.
observations.uncertainty: This is a 65-page OECD working paper and descriptive policy analysis; it does not establish causal effects or show that the Finland pattern transfers unchanged to other countries.
observations.subgroup: Young people, middle-aged adults, older adults, women and men, workers, caregivers, and people experiencing loneliness or mental-health difficulty.
observations.counterinterpretation: Strong national outcomes remain real; the finding is about distribution, sustainability, and changing exposure to risk across life stages rather than a claim that Finland is broadly failing.

denominator.unit: Finland life-course labor and unpaid-work frame

middle_aged_men.value: employment among middle-aged men has declined markedly since 2019, among the largest such declines in the OECD

women_unpaid_work.unit: ratio of women's unpaid work to men's unpaid work

young_transition.value: recent graduates face rising unemployment alongside weaker educational and mental-health outcomes

mental_health.value: mental-health outcomes for young and middle-aged Finns are worse than those of comparable peers

observations.method: Life-course comparison of employment, unpaid work, education, mental health, and transition indicators within OECD benchmarking.
observations.uncertainty: The paper identifies overlapping pressures but does not decompose the relative contributions of labor demand, education, gender norms, family policy, housing, or post-pandemic effects.
observations.subgroup: Middle-aged men, women with unpaid-care responsibilities, recent graduates, young workers, and people outside secure employment.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some employment and unpaid-work differences may reflect life-stage choices or measurement conventions; the policy issue is constrained choice and unequal exposure, not a presumption that all group differences are harmful.

observations.period: 2018-2026; loneliness and social isolation across age groups

denominator.unit: Finland population social-connection frame benchmarked to OECD peers

population_direction.value: loneliness and social isolation increased across all age groups since 2018

older_adults.value: people aged 50 and over saw the largest deterioration, with adults aged 75 and over the most isolated and lonely

young_people.value: young Finns report loneliness at nearly twice the OECD youth average, although levels may be stabilizing after the pandemic peak

policy_implication.value: social connection should be treated as prevention and social investment across the life course

observations.method: OECD analysis of social-connection indicators by age and comparison with OECD averages, linked to prevention and social-investment policy framing.
observations.uncertainty: Loneliness and isolation measures capture related but distinct experiences; the paper does not estimate a causal effect of any single service or community intervention.
observations.subgroup: Young people, adults aged 50 and over, adults aged 75 and over, people living alone, and groups with limited access to social support.
observations.counterinterpretation: Reported loneliness may partly reflect changing norms and disclosure; post-pandemic stabilization would not erase the longer-term deterioration or its unequal distribution.

social_spending.value: pension, health, and long-term-care spending doubled between 2009 and 2022

capacity_pressure.value: aging, debt, defense needs, AI and digitalization create competing demands on future policy capacity

observations.method: OECD demographic, public-finance, social-spending, and forward-looking policy-capacity assessment.
observations.uncertainty: The fiscal figures describe pressure and trade-offs, not a forecast of insolvency or a quantified estimate of the effect of any specific reform.
observations.subgroup: Older adults, working-age taxpayers, families, caregivers, public-service users, and future cohorts affected by demographic and fiscal choices.
observations.counterinterpretation: Demographic pressure can also accelerate productivity, prevention, migration, and service redesign; the report frames capacity as a policy challenge rather than a predetermined decline.

Official OECD DOI and publication citation.

boundary: This record adds a comparative advanced-economy route showing how strong aggregate well-being can coexist with age-specific labor, mental-health, loneliness, gender, and fiscal pressures. It is not a causal evaluation, a respondent-level study, or proof that Finland's policy mix generalizes.
